listen_text: Section. Definition and Properties. In this chapter we introduce the concept of Church—Rosser property and some common properties of this property. Definition. Church—Rosser property, CR. A relation the X arrow relation on terms is said to satisfy the Church—Rosser property if and only if, whenever M is X related to P and M is X related to Q , then there exists some N such that P is X related to N and Q is X related to N . End definition. We can view the lambda calculus as a model of computation in which terms in normal form are “values” and a reducibility relation on terms are the “calculation rules.” The Church—Rosser property states is that when there is more than one way to proceed with a calculation, there is still only a single value of the expression. To take an example from elementary algebra, there's more than one way to calculate four times the quantity one plus two, then plus three . It can either be reduced to four times three, then plus three (if we first reduce one plus two to three ) or to four times one, plus four times two, plus three (if we first reduce four times the quantity one plus two using distributivity). Both of these, however, can be further reduced to twelve plus three . If we take the X arrow relation to be beta -reduction, we easily see that a consequence of the Church—Rosser property is that if a term has a normal form, then it is unique. For suppose M can be reduced to P and Q , both of which are normal forms. By the Church—Rosser property, there exists some N such that both P and Q reduce to it. Since by assumption P and Q are normal forms, the reduction of P and Q to N can only be the trivial reduction, that is, P , Q , and N are identical. This justifies our speaking of the normal form of a term. In viewing the lambda calculus as a model of computation, then, the normal form of a term can be thought of as the “final result” of the computation starting with that term. The above corollary means there's only one, if any, final result of a computation, just like there is only one result of computing four times the quantity one plus two, then plus three , namely fifteen . Theorem. If a relation the X arrow relation satisfies the Church—Rosser property, and the transitive X reduction relation is the smallest transitive relation containing the X arrow relation , then the transitive X reduction relation satisfies the Church—Rosser property too. End theorem. Proof. Suppose Displayed expression. Two chains in the X arrow relation start at M. The first passes through P subscript one and successive P terms through P subscript m. The second passes through Q subscript one and successive Q terms through Q subscript n. Every displayed arrow points forward along its chain. End displayed expression. We will prove the theorem by constructing a grid N of terms of height is m plus one and width n plus one . We use N at row i and column j to denote the term in the i indexed row and j indexed column. We construct N in such a way that N at row i and column j is X related to N at row i plus one and column j and N at row i and column j is X related to N at row i and column j plus one . It is defined as follows: Displayed expression. Grid definition. N at row zero and column zero equals M. N at row i and column zero equals P subscript i, for one less than or equal to i less than or equal to m. N at row zero and column j equals Q subscript j, for one less than or equal to j less than or equal to n. Otherwise, N at row i and column j equals R, the common successor specified immediately after this display. End of grid definition. End displayed expression. where R is a term such that N at row i minus one and column j is X related to R and N at row i and column j minus one is X related to R . By the Church—Rosser property of the X arrow relation , such a term always exists. Now we have a forward chain in the X arrow relation along row m, from N at row m and column zero through successive columns to N at row m and column n and a forward chain in the X arrow relation along column n, from N at row zero and column n through successive rows to N at row m and column n . Note N at row m and column zero is P and N at row zero and column n is Q . By definition of the transitive X reduction relation the theorem follows. End proof. End section.

Definition. parallel beta -reduction, parallel beta reduction . Parallel reduction ( parallel beta reduction ) of terms is inductively defined as follows: List. Next item. x parallel beta reduces to x . Next item. If N beta reduces in one step to N prime then the lambda abstraction binding x with body N parallel beta reduces to the lambda abstraction binding x with body N prime . Next item. If P parallel beta reduces to P prime and Q parallel beta reduces to Q prime then the application of P to Q parallel beta reduces to the application of P prime to Q prime . Next item. If N parallel beta reduces to N prime and Q parallel beta reduces to Q prime then the application to Q of the lambda abstraction binding x with body N parallel beta reduces to the result of substituting Q prime for free x in N prime . End list. End definition. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. The abstraction rule's premise is printed with an ordinary one step beta arrow, not a parallel beta arrow. Later proofs use a parallel beta premise. The displayed rule is preserved, not silently changed. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Parallel beta -reduction allows us to reduce any number of redices in a term in one step. It is different from beta -reduction in the sense that we can only contract redices that occur in the original term, but not redices arising from parallel beta -reduction. For example, the term the application of the lambda abstraction binding f with body f applied to x, to the lambda abstraction binding y with body y can only be parallel beta -reduced to itself or to the application to x of the lambda abstraction binding y with body y , but not further to x , although it beta -reduces to x , because this redex arises only after one step of parallel beta -reduction. A second parallel beta -reduction step yields x , though. Theorem. M parallel beta reduces to M . End theorem. Proof. Exercise. End proof. Exercise. Prove the theorem on reflexivity of parallel beta reduction . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Definition. beta -complete development. The beta -complete development the beta complete development of M of M is defined inductively as follows: Displayed expression. Beta complete development, four defining equations. One: the beta complete development of x equals x. Two: the beta complete development of the lambda abstraction binding x with body N equals the lambda abstraction binding x with body the beta complete development of N. Three: the beta complete development of the application of P to Q equals the application of the beta complete development of P to the beta complete development of Q, if P is not a lambda abstraction. Four: the beta complete development of the application to Q of the lambda abstraction binding x with body N equals the result of substituting the beta complete development of Q for free x in the beta complete development of N. End of the four equations. End displayed expression. End definition. The beta -complete development of a term, as its name suggests, is a “complete parallel reduction.” While for parallel beta -reduction we still can choose to not contract a redex, for complete development we have no choice but to contract all of them. Thus the complete development of the application of the lambda abstraction binding f with body f applied to x, to the lambda abstraction binding y with body y is the application to x of the lambda abstraction binding y with body y , not itself.
